deed: יעקב בן מכיר אבן תיבון ממונפלייה תיאר את רובע ישראל — רובע אסטרונומי מהמצאתו שלו
title: The Quadrant of Israel of Jacob ben Makhir ibn Tibbon

trailer.text: Jacob ben Makhir ibn Tibbon, known also as Don Profeit Tibbon, was a Jewish scholar who lived in Montpellier and in other towns in Provence.
He translated Arabic scientific works into Hebrew and also wrote a few original astronomical works.
According to MacTutor, in one of them he described a quadrant of his own invention.
According to DSB, the work on the Quadrant of Israel was written in Hebrew between 1288 and 1293, and was translated into Latin in 1299.
In Latin the instrument was called Quadrans Novus, and according to Vernet examples of it have been preserved and it apparently was much used in its time.

glance.label: Who
glance.value: A Jewish scholar from Provence, translator and astronomer

glance.label: What
glance.value: The Quadrant of Israel, in Latin Quadrans Novus

paragraphs.text: The Ibn Tibbon family, from which Jacob came, came from Granada.
In 1150 his great-grandfather, Judah ben Saul ibn Tibbon, moved to the south of France because of the unrest in Granada.

According to the DSB, the family's translations were among the most important cultural works of the time, at least from a historical point of view, because they were part of the process through which Arabic knowledge, and through it the Greek scientific traditions, were made accessible to the scholars of medieval Europe.
According to MacTutor, Jacob was the son of Machir ben Judah ibn Tibbon, was born in Marseilles, and continued the family tradition in medicine and translation.
According to Muslim Heritage, he was born, probably in Marseilles, about 1236.

stations.title: Physician and student in Provence and Spain

paragraphs.text: Jacob was educated in Lunel and then studied medicine in the medical faculty of the University of Montpellier.
According to DSB, it appears that from 1266 to 1267 he lived in Gerona, Spain, as a follower of Moses ben Nahman.
According to MacTutor, he returned to Lunel, where he had family connections, and also lived for long periods in Montpellier.
He spent most of his life in Lunel and Montpellier.
According to MacTutor he was a French Jewish medical doctor, and according to Muslim Heritage he was highly reputed as a physician.
Jacob wrote exclusively in Hebrew.
His translations were almost entirely of mathematical and astronomical works, both original Arabic tracts and Arabic versions of Greek works.
According to DSB, he translated, among others, Autolycus, Euclid and Menelaus.
He also produced Hebrew versions of the works of philosophers, including Ibn Rushd.
In the introduction to his translation of Euclid's Elements, he wrote that he translated the book to avoid the mockery of the Christians, "who say that we lack to all sciences".
Ideologically he adhered to the Maimonidean philosophy.
In the controversy between the Maimonists and the anti-Maimonists he defended science against the attacks of Abba Mari and his party.

stations.title: The Quadrant of Israel: a new instrument

paragraphs.text: Jacob's two original works were on the quadrant and an almanac.
According to MacTutor, in the work Quadrant of Jacob he described a quadrant of his own invention.
According to DSB, the work was written in Hebrew between 1288 and 1293.
According to Vernet, the instrument is a simplification of the face of the astrolabe by means of two successive folds whose axes are the north-south and east-west lines.
The work contains a table of fixed stars to be used in the construction of the instrument.
According to DSB, Armengaud, son of Blaise, translated the work into Latin in 1299.
In Latin it was called Quadrans Novus, and the work was translated widely into Latin.
In 1301 an expansion of the work appeared.
Its Hebrew text has been lost, and it is preserved in the Latin translation by Peter of St.-Omer, from about 1309, which was translated back into Hebrew.
According to the Biographical Encyclopedia, the work on the quadrant had a wide influence from the last decade of the 13th century.
According to Vernet, examples of the instrument have been preserved, and it apparently was much used in its time.
The second original work was an almanac, in Hebrew "Luhot".
According to the author, it was based on a similar work by Zarqali, and was calculated according to the Toledan Tables, with a change of meridian from Toledo to Montpellier.
According to MacTutor, the almanac was written for users in Montpellier, indicating that Jacob was living and working there.
In the almanac, the table of the corrected equation of the Moon is given daily, from 22 March 1300, for 23 years.

stations.title: A name that reached the Renaissance

paragraphs.text: Jacob ben Makhir was influential long after his time, which is perhaps surprising in view of his surviving writings.
According to DSB, his astronomical work was very highly regarded during the Renaissance, and he was cited by Copernicus, Reinhold, Clavius and Kepler.
According to Muslim Heritage, his works were translated into Latin and quoted by Copernicus, Reinhold and Clavius.
Copernicus attributes to him a value of the obliquity of the ecliptic for 1290.
In Romance languages he was known as Don Profiat or Profeit, and in Latin as Prophatius Judaeus.
Since he was known under two Hebrew names, modern scholars treated them as two separate persons, until Salomon Munk showed that they were one person.
According to MacTutor, Jacob was much more than a translator: a fine mathematician and astronomer who also wrote original works in addition to the translations.
According to Muslim Heritage, he died in Montpellier about 1304.
According to MacTutor, there has been a considerable debate among historians as to the basis for the tables in the almanac.
Pierre Duhem criticised Jacob for using old tables instead of the latest available to him.
Later astronomers found errors in his work and corrected them.
According to the Biographical Encyclopedia, the value of the obliquity of the ecliptic that Copernicus attributes to him has not been traced to any surviving text.

disagreements.question: On what date do the almanac's tables begin?

versions.says: According to the Biographical Encyclopedia, the Sun table begins on 1 March 1301, and the tables of the outer planets on 10 March 1300
According to the DSB, the almanac is dated 1 March 1300 (that is, 1301 AD)
According to MacTutor, the calculations begin with data for March 1300

disagreements.question: What was the relationship between Jacob and Samuel ben Judah ibn Tibbon?

According to Muslim Heritage, Jacob was a grandson of Samuel ben Judah ibn Tibbon

disagreements.question: On which tables was the almanac based?

versions.says: According to Jacob himself, he followed the method of his predecessors, using the Toledan Tables as a basis
According to DSB, this explanation is not quite correct
Several writers, among them Andalo di Negro, believed that he had used the Alfonsine Tables
Toomer concluded that Jacob did indeed use the Toledan Tables as the basis
